cells.tense: You are at the table with what you grew, and you can see it is good.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you tended that is bearing something now, out loud, to someone who watched you do it. Then let yourself have it for a day.
cells.core: You are at the table with what you grew, and it is actually good. You didn't force the timing. You fed it, kept it alive, and it came in on its own. That is what flourishing looks like from the inside, plain and a little surprising.\n\nThe next thing to feed is one you've been circling, the one that feels a little more yours than the rest. Keep tending it the same way you tended the others, no special push. This stays a balance because you can tell what is done and what only looks like it. When that line gets blurry, you start holding on past the moment it should be let go.
cells.sheetLine: What you tended is ripe. Pick it up and hold it.
cells.verb: tending what is alive until it comes into its own
cells.place: where what you are is allowed to show without dimming

cells.tense: You are bracing for a season that has not arrived, and the bracing is already costing you.
cells.ask: Let one thing you have been pushing finish without your hand on it. Close the gate for a day and see what comes through.
cells.core: You are doing the work of the next season before this one is done. The push lives in the future. You are standing over a patch that is not ready and trying to make it yield from here, and that standing is what wears the care thin.\n\nThe better fuel is not more pushing. It is letting one thing finish on its own and seeing what it actually becomes. You can do that without staking yourself on how it goes. It tests the ground, not you. What you tend needs room to come in, and it doesn't need you standing there while it does. Try it, and watch what holds.
cells.sheetLine: You are forcing a harvest that has not finished growing.
cells.verb: tending what is alive until it comes into its own
cells.place: where what you are is allowed to show without dimming

cells.tense: You are still standing at the door of what you planted, and that door is behind you.
cells.ask: Pick one direction to steer by for the next month and take a small step toward it. Choose it tonight; the size of the step doesn't matter.
cells.core: You know how to tend things, but tending stopped feeling like yours to do. Something back there made the work feel unsafe to carry forward, and you keep waiting at a gate that already opened. The soil is not the problem. The standing is.\n\nThere is no harvest to point at until you start again, and starting looks like choosing one real thing and moving the next small step toward it. That brings the reach back first; the shining comes in last. Say the first step out loud to one other person. Worth will not follow a performance, and you have no performance in you. You don't have to feel like it yet.
cells.sheetLine: The movement starts before the shine comes back.

cells.tense: The thing is already growing through your hands, and you are telling yourself it grew by itself.
cells.ask: Say 'this is mine' out loud about one piece of it — the one you credit to the work, the season, or someone else. Say it once and mean it.
cells.core: You already did the thing you're looking for evidence of. It runs through your hands every week: the watering, the waiting, the cutting back. You talk about it like it happened to you. The hands are doing it; the pen just hasn't been picked up yet.\n\nThere is an earlier, simpler form of this same work still available to you. Go back to what it was before it got folded into everything else, and call it yours there. Keeping something alive doesn't need a title to be true. When you say it, you aren't inflating anything. You're signing what is already on the page.
cells.sheetLine: The growing is already yours. Sign it.

attempts.check: The record gives no evidence that what this person tended is actually bearing fruit in their outer life, so the reading must describe the capacity for tending, not assert a harvest. The reader could reasonably say the garden is not flourishing at all, but the ask still holds: noticing something they grew and fed works whether the crop is rich or poor. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying they have already arrived.
